title: Web Protocols & Security
description: HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3, CORS, WebSockets, CSRF/XSS, JWT deep, OAuth 2.0 flows, TLS, security headers. Turing FDE Stage 1 MCQ heavy focus.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is IDEMPOTENT but NOT safe?
questions.explanation: Safe = no state change (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). Idempotent = same result on retry (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE). PUT is idempotent but changes state.

questions.prompt: 422 Unprocessable Entity means:

options.text: The request is well-formed but semantically invalid (e.g., validation failed)

questions.explanation: 400 = malformed. 422 = well-formed but rejected by application logic. 409 = conflict.

questions.prompt: Which are TRUE about HTTP/2? (select all)

options.text: Multiplexes multiple streams over one TCP connection

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 = multiplexed streams + binary framing + HPACK on TCP. Server push exists but has been deprecated by most browsers. HTTP/3 moves to UDP (QUIC).

questions.prompt: The biggest reason HTTP/3 uses QUIC (UDP) over TCP is:

options.text: Eliminates head-of-line blocking at the transport layer + faster connection setup (0-RTT resume)

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 still had TCP HOL blocking (one lost packet blocks all streams). QUIC handles streams independently at UDP + integrates TLS 1.3 handshake.

questions.prompt: A browser makes `fetch('https://api.example.com/data', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }})` from origin `app.example.com`. What happens first?

options.text: Browser sends an OPTIONS preflight because Content-Type isn't in the simple-request list
CORS is skipped for same eTLD+1
The server sees no request at all

questions.explanation: Non-simple requests (custom headers, methods other than GET/HEAD/POST-simple, non-basic Content-Type) trigger preflight. Server must respond with Access-Control-Allow-* headers to proceed.

questions.prompt: Which are needed for `fetch(..., { credentials: 'include' })` to work cross-origin? (select all)
questions.explanation: With credentials, `*` is disallowed for Allow-Origin; must echo the origin exactly. Cookies also need SameSite=None and Secure for cross-site sending.

questions.prompt: You control the frontend and backend. Why choose CORS-with-credentials over sending a Bearer token in the Authorization header?

options.text: Cookies with HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite are not accessible to JS → immune to XSS token theft; Bearer tokens in JS are XSS-vulnerable
Bearer tokens don't work with CORS

questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies can't be exfiltrated by XSS. The trade-off: CSRF risk resurfaces, so use SameSite + CSRF tokens.

questions.prompt: The WebSocket handshake starts as:

options.text: A raw TCP connection with a custom protocol
An HTTP GET with `Upgrade: websocket` header, negotiating up to a WebSocket connection

questions.explanation: Client sends HTTP 1.1 Upgrade → server responds 101 Switching Protocols → same TCP stays open with WebSocket frames.

questions.prompt: When would you choose Server-Sent Events (SSE) over WebSockets?

options.text: One-way server → client push (notifications, dashboards) + you want to leverage HTTP infra + auto-reconnect built in
You need lower latency than WS
SSE is a superset of WS

questions.explanation: SSE = simpler protocol over HTTP; unidirectional; browser handles reconnect + Last-Event-ID. WS is bidirectional and binary-capable.

questions.prompt: You have a WS server behind a load balancer. Clients report random disconnects after 60s of silence. Likely cause?

options.text: LB idle-timeout kills long-lived connections without traffic — add ping/pong heartbeats

questions.explanation: AWS ELB defaults to 60s idle timeout. Send WS ping frames (or app-level pings) every ~30s.

questions.prompt: To scale WebSockets across N app nodes so any client can receive a message about any topic, you need:

options.text: A pub/sub backbone (Redis/NATS/Kafka) so any node can publish; nodes subscribe on behalf of their connected clients

questions.explanation: Connections are stateful — the node holding a client's socket must receive relevant messages. Pub/sub decouples publishers from where the recipient's socket lives.

questions.prompt: Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH) is prevented by:

options.text: Server-side Origin header validation (WS doesn't have same-origin policy) + short-lived auth tokens rather than cookies

questions.explanation: The browser sends Origin on the handshake; server MUST check it. Cookies auto-attach, so CSWSH is essentially CSRF-over-WS.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid CSRF defense that does NOT require server-stored state?
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax|Strict blocks cross-site cookie sending on top-level nav and subresources. Double-submit-cookie is another stateless option. Synchronizer token requires server state.

questions.prompt: Which mitigate XSS? (select all)

options.text: Escape output based on context (HTML text, HTML attribute, JS, CSS, URL)
Content Security Policy that blocks inline scripts (`script-src 'self'`)
Use HttpOnly cookies so JS can't read auth tokens
Sanitize HTML with an allowlist library (DOMPurify)

questions.explanation: Defense-in-depth. CORS doesn't stop XSS. Framework auto-escaping helps but not for `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`/`v-html`/`innerHTML`.

questions.prompt: You render user-supplied Markdown to HTML with a library. What's the residual risk?

options.text: Markdown allows raw HTML by default in most libraries — sanitize the OUTPUT with DOMPurify
Only if the user is admin

questions.explanation: marked/markdown-it pass HTML through unless configured otherwise. Even 'safe' modes have escaped in the past — always sanitize the rendered HTML.

questions.prompt: A strict CSP typically includes:
questions.explanation: Nonce-based CSP blocks inline unless the nonce matches; frame-ancestors prevents clickjacking; default-src 'self' locks to same origin.

questions.prompt: A JWT's three parts (`header.payload.signature`) are separated by `.` and each is:
questions.explanation: Base64url (no padding, URL-safe). Signature is HMAC or RSA/ECDSA. Encryption exists as JWE — different spec.

questions.prompt: Which are REAL JWT vulnerabilities? (select all)

options.text: `alg: none` attack if server doesn't enforce algorithm
RS256 → HS256 confusion attack (server verifies HMAC using the public key)
Weak secret guessed via offline brute force
Token can't be revoked mid-expiry without server state

questions.explanation: All real. Mitigations: pin algorithm, keep secrets long/random, short expiry + refresh tokens with revocation store.

questions.prompt: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow order (client, auth server, resource):

options.text: User → auth server (login/consent) → redirect back with code → client exchanges code for tokens at token endpoint → uses access_token at resource

questions.explanation: Code-then-exchange is the canonical flow. PKCE adds a code_verifier for public clients.

questions.prompt: OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds what to OAuth 2.0?

options.text: An `id_token` (a JWT with user identity claims) alongside the access_token

questions.explanation: OIDC turns OAuth (authorization) into an authentication protocol via id_token + userinfo endpoint.

questions.prompt: SAML is chosen over OIDC when:

options.text: Enterprise IdP (Okta/AD FS/Ping) integrates with legacy SP that speaks XML-based SAML assertions

questions.explanation: SAML is XML-heavy but ubiquitous in enterprise SSO. OIDC is the modern choice for greenfield.

questions.prompt: TLS 1.3 vs 1.2 key difference:

options.text: 1-RTT handshake (0-RTT resume), removed weak ciphers, mandatory forward secrecy

questions.explanation: Faster + safer defaults. QUIC uses TLS 1.3 baked in.

questions.prompt: Certificate pinning is useful for:

options.text: Mobile apps talking to your own backend, to resist rogue CAs / MITM

questions.explanation: Pinning breaks legitimate cert rotation. HPKP (browser pinning) was deprecated. Use CAA + monitoring for public web.

questions.prompt: Which security headers do you want on a typical web app? (select all)
questions.explanation: X-XSS-Protection is deprecated / disabled in modern browsers. Others are standard. helmet in Express ships good defaults.

questions.prompt: `SameSite=Strict` cookie:

options.text: Is sent on all cross-site requests
Is NOT sent on any cross-site request — including top-level navigation from another site (breaks 'log in via link from email')

questions.explanation: Strict blocks EVERY cross-site send. Lax allows top-level GET navigation. None requires Secure + explicit opt-in.

questions.prompt: For a versioned bundle like `app.abc123.js`, the ideal cache header is:
questions.explanation: Fingerprinted asset = never changes → cache forever. HTML wrapper stays no-cache so users get new asset URL fast.

questions.prompt: A REST API `GET /users/123` returns 200 with a body, but a proxy caches it forever ignoring the app's expected freshness. Root cause candidate:
questions.explanation: Without explicit Cache-Control, intermediaries may heuristically cache (esp. GET 200 with Last-Modified). Set `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` or `no-store` for user-specific responses.

questions.prompt: REST vs GraphQL — GraphQL wins when:

options.text: Clients need flexible shapes + few round trips + heavy nested data + a single evolving schema

questions.explanation: GraphQL centralizes over-fetch/under-fetch pain. REST wins on caching + simplicity + tooling.

questions.prompt: gRPC advantages over REST/JSON include (best answer):

options.text: Binary Protobuf + HTTP/2 multiplexing + strongly-typed contracts + streaming, at the cost of browser compat requiring gRPC-Web
Better for public APIs than REST

questions.explanation: Great for service-to-service. Browsers need gRPC-Web proxy since raw HTTP/2 trailers aren't exposed to fetch().

questions.prompt: A user reports intermittent 502s from your API. First thing to check:

options.text: Upstream health: origin timeouts, connection resets, unhealthy pods, LB idle timeout vs keep-alive mismatch

questions.explanation: 502 = bad gateway = the LB/reverse proxy got a bad reply from origin. Usually app pods crashing, timeouts, or keep-alive mismatch.

questions.prompt: You accept `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` on a JSON API and skip preflight. What breaks security?

options.text: Any HTML page can POST to your API without preflight (simple request), enabling CSRF against cookie-authed endpoints

questions.explanation: Simple-request content types skip preflight, and any form can submit them cross-origin. Prefer JSON-only + require preflight + SameSite cookies.

questions.prompt: You use an ORM. Which pattern still risks SQL injection?

options.text: `sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ${email}`` (tagged-template with proper lib)

questions.explanation: String interpolation into raw SQL — even inside an ORM — is unsafe. Parameterization or safe tagged templates prevent injection.

questions.prompt: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) mitigations include: (select all)

options.text: Resolve DNS ONCE and connect to that IP (prevent TOCTOU rebinding)
Trust user-supplied URLs after regex check
Run image/URL fetchers in a separate, isolated network segment

questions.explanation: Regex-only fails on DNS rebinding + URL parsing quirks. Layer defenses.

questions.prompt: For a public API, per-IP rate limiting alone is weak because:

options.text: NAT + CGNAT + proxies share one IP among many users; attackers can rotate IPs via proxy pools

questions.explanation: Combine per-IP + per-API-key + per-user + WAF signals. Cloudflare/AWS WAF handle much of this.

questions.prompt: You cut over to a new API host. Some users still hit the old one 24h later. Fix in advance:

options.text: Lower the DNS TTL well before cutover (e.g., 60s) so caches expire fast

questions.explanation: TTL controls resolver cache lifetime. Prep with 60–300s TTL a few days ahead; restore normal TTL post-cutover.

questions.prompt: Ideal 'connect timeout' vs 'read timeout' for calls to an internal microservice:

options.text: Short connect (1–2s), longer but bounded read (5–15s); always set BOTH

questions.explanation: No-timeout clients starve pools during upstream outages. Node's fetch has AbortController; axios has connect + read.

questions.prompt: You need to stream JSON to a browser as it's generated. Use:

options.text: Chunked Transfer-Encoding + NDJSON (one JSON object per line) OR SSE

questions.explanation: NDJSON is the common streaming JSON convention. SSE is fine if you want built-in reconnect and event framing.

questions.prompt: You're receiving webhooks from Stripe. Best signature verification approach:

options.text: Compute HMAC over the raw body + timestamp header with your webhook secret, constant-time compare, reject stale timestamps

questions.explanation: Must use raw body — parsing then reserializing changes bytes. Constant-time compare avoids timing attacks. Reject events older than a few minutes.

questions.prompt: Refresh token rotation means:

options.text: Each refresh returns a NEW refresh + access token; using an old refresh invalidates the family (defends against stolen refresh)

questions.explanation: Rotation + reuse detection is the OWASP-recommended flow. Auth0/Cognito/Supabase all default to it.

questions.prompt: For handling secrets in a production Node app:

options.text: Commit `.env` to git in a private repo
Load from secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Vault) at boot; never commit

questions.explanation: Secret manager + IAM role. Image env vars leak in `docker inspect`; CLI args in `ps`.
